options: An IAM user in each account with matching long-lived keys for the integration.
A user account whose long-lived keys the bucket's configuration embeds for signing each event it sends.
A cron job on a server that scans the complete bucket listing and invokes the function for unprocessed objects.
The function's resource-based policy, which allows the S3 principal to invoke it with the bucket as source.
questions.correct_rationale: A resource-based policy on the function grants the S3 service principal invocation permission scoped to the bucket, keeping the grant with the resource.
distractor_rationales: Duplicated long-lived keys across accounts multiply secrets to rotate and leak.
Embedded user keys are long-lived secrets in configuration, which the requirement excludes.
A scanning cron job replaces the event-driven trigger and adds lag.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options embed secrets, scan instead of reacting, or multiply long-lived keys.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Implement authentication and authorization mechanisms for applications and AWS services
questions.question: An identity pool serves two kinds of sign-in: partner tokens from an external provider and employee tokens from the corporate directory. Partners must receive a limited role and employees a broader role, chosen automatically per sign-in. Which identity pool feature fits?
options: Role mapping rules that select the role per sign-in from the token's claims.
One shared role whose IAM policy inspects the caller's user agent at request time.
Separate identity pools per partner, each with a copy of the app's configuration.
Hard-coded role selection in the application based on a flag set at registration.
questions.correct_rationale: Role mapping rules in the identity pool choose the assumed role from token claims, per sign-in, automatically.
distractor_rationales: User-agent inspection inside a shared role is unreliable and evaluates on every call rather than at credential issuance.
One pool per partner multiplies configuration and drift.
Application-side flag selection bypasses the identity layer and cannot be trusted.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options inspect at the wrong time, multiply pools, or move trust into app flags.

questions.subdomain: 3.1 Prepare application artifacts to be deployed to AWS
questions.question: A container registry receives images from many teams. Security requires that images are scanned for vulnerabilities when they are pushed, so findings surface before any deployment references them. Which ECR capability fits?
options: Disabling image pulls until a third-party scanner contract is signed.
A quarterly external penetration test of the deployed containers.
A nightly manual review of the image tags by the platform team.
Scan-on-push scanning of each image as it enters the repository.
questions.correct_rationale: Scan-on-push scans images at upload time and reports findings, so vulnerabilities surface before deployment.
distractor_rationales: Blocking pulls halts the platform instead of scanning it.
Penetration tests assess running deployments, not registry images at push time.
Manual tag review sees names, not vulnerabilities.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options test the wrong stage, review by hand, or halt deliveries.

questions.subdomain: 3.1 Prepare application artifacts to be deployed to AWS
questions.question: One CloudFormation template defines the application stack for development, staging, and production. Which template feature passes the differing values — such as instance counts — per environment without editing the template per deployment?
options: Template parameters with per-deployment values supplied at create or update time.
Three copies of the template, one per environment, kept in sync by hand.
Hard-coding the production values in the template and letting the other environments tolerate them.
Commenting values in and out of the template before each deployment.
questions.correct_rationale: Parameters make one template serve every environment, with values supplied per deployment.
distractor_rationales: Hand-synced copies drift the moment one environment changes.
Hard-coded values cannot vary per environment at all.
Comment toggling is an error-prone manual edit of the template.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options copy, hard-code, or manually toggle the template instead of parameterizing it.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 Deploy code by using AWS continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) services
questions.question: A service on ECS deploys new task definitions several times a day. When a deployment's tasks fail health checks, the platform must roll the service back to the previous task definition without an engineer watching. Which mechanism fits?
options: A scheduled task that compares current and previous task definitions and redeploys on mismatch.
The ECS deployment circuit breaker, which rolls back automatically when a deployment fails.
A support runbook that an engineer executes during business hours.
Deleting the service and redeploying the last known good task definition.
questions.correct_rationale: The deployment circuit breaker detects failed deployments and automatically rolls the service back to the last healthy state.
distractor_rationales: A scheduled comparator is custom machinery that reacts after users notice.
A business-hours runbook leaves failed deployments serving until someone reads the page.
Delete-and-redeploy drops traffic and depends on a human remembering the last good definition.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options watch, page, or drop traffic instead of rolling back automatically.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 Deploy code by using AWS continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) services
questions.question: An application runs on instances tagged by tier — batch and web. Releases must deploy to the batch tier and web tier on different schedules with different failure handling, using one application definition. Which CodeDeploy construct fits?
options: One deployment group covering all instances, deploying everywhere at once.
Two deployment groups under one application, each selecting its tier by instance tag.
Two separate applications with duplicated revisions and unrelated histories.
A shell script that reads the instance tags and applies releases by hand.
questions.correct_rationale: Deployment groups select targets by tag under one application, so each tier deploys on its own configuration and schedule.
distractor_rationales: One all-instance group cannot give tiers different schedules or failure handling.
Duplicated applications fork the revision history the single-definition requirement keeps unified.
A tag-reading script is the hand-rolled targeting CodeDeploy provides.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options merge the tiers, fork the application, or script the targeting manually.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 Deploy code by using AWS continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) services
questions.question: A platform team must roll out a baseline IAM configuration to dozens of accounts across several Regions, with each account's stack staying updatable from one place. Which CloudFormation capability fits?
options: An S3 bucket holding the template for each account's engineers to apply manually.
Copying the template into each account and deploying it separately by hand.
CloudFormation StackSets, which deploys one template across many accounts and Regions.
Mailing the template to each account owner for local execution.
questions.correct_rationale: StackSets deploys and updates a template across multiple accounts and Regions from one definition.
distractor_rationales: A shared bucket only stores templates; it deploys nothing.
Per-account manual deployment drifts and has no central update path.
Mailing templates is not an update mechanism.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options distribute files or rely on humans instead of deploying centrally.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 Deploy code by using AWS continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) services
questions.question: A stack's resources were modified outside CloudFormation, and the team suspects manual console changes but cannot name which resources differ from the template. Which capability identifies them?
options: A monthly meeting where each engineer denies making console changes to the stack.
Deleting the stack and recreating it from the template to eliminate unknown changes by force.
Reading the template file and the console side by side, hoping the differences become obvious.
CloudFormation drift detection, which compares deployed resources against the template and reports the differences.
questions.correct_rationale: Drift detection compares the deployed resources with the template and reports which resources and properties changed outside it.
distractor_rationales: A denial meeting produces no evidence.
Recreating the stack destroys the evidence along with the workload.
Reading the template shows intent, not the deployed state.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options destroy, guess, or meet instead of detecting the differences.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 Deploy code by using AWS continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) services
questions.question: A pipeline builds in a tooling account and must deploy to a separate production account. The production deploy must use the production account's own role, and the artifact must transfer securely between accounts. Which pipeline configuration fits?
options: Separate pipelines per account, with the built artifact emailed between the teams.
One pipeline that runs entirely inside the tooling account and uses the engineer's personal credentials for the production deploys.
A cross-account pipeline whose production stage assumes a role in the production account, with a shared artifact store.
Deploying from the tooling account after making the production account trust every principal in it.
questions.correct_rationale: Cross-account pipelines stage artifacts in a shared store and assume per-account roles, so each deployment runs under the target account's permissions.
distractor_rationales: Emailing artifacts has no integrity or audit story.
Personal credentials in a pipeline are unscoped, unrotated, and unaccountable.
Broad trust for every principal is the vulnerability the design must close.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options deploy with personal keys, mail artifacts, or grant blanket trust.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 Deploy code by using AWS continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) services
questions.question: A team's code lives in a third-party hosted repository. The pipeline must trigger on commits without any long-lived credentials for the repository stored in AWS. Which mechanism fits?
options: A long-lived personal access token stored in a pipeline variable for source polling.
A CodePipeline connection to the third-party source using the connections feature, which authorizes via the provider's app.
A scheduled export of the repository into an S3 bucket for the pipeline to poll.
A web page the team checks by hand to start deployments after each push to the repository.
questions.correct_rationale: Connections authorize the third-party provider through its app integration, so commits trigger the pipeline without stored tokens.
distractor_rationales: A stored personal access token is the long-lived credential the requirement excludes.
Scheduled exports add lag and copy the repository without a trigger path.
Manual checks defeat the automatic triggering the pipeline exists for.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options store tokens, copy with lag, or rely on humans to notice commits.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 Deploy code by using AWS continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) services
questions.question: An application deploy must run a database schema migration exactly once, after new code is on the instances but before they receive traffic. A failed migration must fail the deployment before any user sees the new version. Which CodeDeploy mechanism orders this correctly?
options: Running the migration by hand from an engineer's workstation during the deployment window.
A nightly scheduled migration job that runs ahead of the deployment window regardless of whether a deploy happens.
A lifecycle hook before the traffic shift whose script runs the migration and fails the deployment on error.
An after-traffic hook that migrates the schema while users are already exercising the new code.
questions.correct_rationale: Lifecycle hooks order scripts around the traffic shift; a pre-traffic hook runs the migration once per deployment and failing it stops the rollout.
distractor_rationales: Manual workstation migrations are unrepeatable and unaudited.
A nightly job cannot know when a deploy happens and races it.
After-traffic hooks run the migration while users already hit the new code.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options race the deploy, run by hand, or migrate after exposure.

questions.subdomain: 3.1 Prepare application artifacts to be deployed to AWS
questions.question: A new checkout path must ship dark to a fraction of users, with the ability to disable it instantly if error rates rise — without a deployment. Which mechanism fits?
options: An AppConfig feature flag deployed with a gradual rollout strategy, read by the application at runtime.
A second Lambda function version that the team switches to by redeploying the API.
A configuration file baked into the container image and refreshed through a new release each time.
A spreadsheet of enabled users that support edits by ticket any time the list changes.
questions.correct_rationale: Feature flags in AppConfig release behavior gradually to a user fraction and can be disabled immediately without any redeployment.
distractor_rationales: Redeploying a function version is a deployment, which instant disablement excludes.
Baked configuration changes only with a new image build.
A support-edited spreadsheet is neither a rollout mechanism nor fast.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options redeploy, rebuild, or hand-edit instead of flipping a managed flag.

questions.subdomain: 4.2 Apply logging, monitoring, and observability best practices
questions.question: An ordering API's failure was reported by customers 40 minutes before any internal alert fired, because no user had triggered the right alerting conditions internally. The team wants scheduled, scripted user-journey checks against the endpoint. Which mechanism fits?
options: A nightly manual test of the endpoint run by the engineer on duty from a laptop.
A CloudWatch alarm on the API's error metric raised after failures accumulate.
Waiting for the first customer report of each new failure to arrive.
CloudWatch Synthetics canaries that run the user journey on a schedule and alarm on failure.
questions.correct_rationale: Synthetics canaries run scripted user journeys on a schedule and alarm when the journey fails, catching breakage before customers do.
distractor_rationales: A nightly manual test checks once a day and depends on a person.
An error-metric alarm fires only when real user traffic fails, which is the gap being closed.
Waiting for customers is the current broken process.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options react to user traffic, user reports, or a once-daily check instead of scripted journeys.

questions.subdomain: 4.1 Assist in a root cause analysis
questions.question: An on-call engineer must find every trace in the past day where the payment region was 'eu' and latency exceeded two seconds, filtering traces directly in the X-Ray console. Which X-Ray feature makes traces searchable by such values?
options: Metadata, which stores arbitrary key-value content on segments for reading in trace detail.
Annotations, which are indexed key-value records on segments and searchable in the console.
Debug logging on the payment function with correlation IDs.
A CloudWatch alarm on the payment function's duration metric.
questions.correct_rationale: Annotations are indexed on segments and searchable, so filtered trace discovery works in the console.
distractor_rationales: Metadata is viewable but not indexed for search, which is the filtering need.
Debug logs must be searched outside X-Ray and correlate poorly.
A duration alarm pages on threshold; it does not retrieve traces by attribute.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options store without indexing, scatter the data, or alarm instead of searching.

questions.subdomain: 4.2 Apply logging, monitoring, and observability best practices
questions.question: An EC2 fleet's memory usage is invisible in CloudWatch, and the team needs instance-level memory and disk metrics alongside logs in one place. Which mechanism supplies both?
options: Guessing memory pressure indirectly from the CPU metrics alone when slowness appears.
The default EC2 metrics, which include memory usage for every instance automatically.
A script on each instance that emails a daily memory graph to the operations inbox by hand.
The CloudWatch agent, installed on the instances, which collects memory, disk, and log data into CloudWatch.
questions.correct_rationale: The CloudWatch agent collects instance-level memory and disk metrics plus logs into CloudWatch from one installed component.
distractor_rationales: CPU correlation is a guess, not a memory measurement.
Default EC2 metrics do not include memory, which is the missing signal.
Daily email graphs are not queryable monitoring.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options assume metrics that do not exist, email graphs, or infer from the wrong signal.

questions.subdomain: 4.3 Optimize applications by using AWS services and features
questions.question: A workflow type runs millions of times per day; each run is short, high-volume, and uses idempotent steps that tolerate a run executing more than once with event history retained briefly for debugging. Cost per run matters more than long-running durability. Which workflow type fits?
options: A Step Functions Standard workflow that batches multiple logical runs into one execution.
Step Functions Standard workflows with parallel states to speed each run.
Step Functions Standard workflows with reduced logging to save cost.
Step Functions Express workflows, designed for high-volume, short-duration runs at lower cost.
questions.correct_rationale: Express workflows trade the Standard durability model for high-volume, short-duration execution at lower per-run cost, with short history retention.
distractor_rationales: Batching logical runs into one execution distorts semantics and error handling.
Parallel states speed work inside a run but keep the Standard per-transition cost model.
Lowering logging does not change the per-run cost structure.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options tweak Standard or distort semantics instead of choosing the Express execution model.

docLinks.title: Choosing workflow type in Step Functions

questions.subdomain: 4.1 Assist in a root cause analysis
questions.question: Clients intermittently receive 504 responses from an application load balancer. Targets report healthy, and the application's own logs show no errors. Which cause matches a load balancer 504 with healthy targets?
options: The load balancer's TLS certificate expiring in the middle of an in-flight request.
Targets responding slower than the idle timeout, so the load balancer gives up waiting.
Clients sending requests with malformed headers that the targets reject immediately.
The targets' security groups blocking the routine health checks the load balancer sends them.
questions.correct_rationale: A 504 from the load balancer with healthy targets means the target did not answer within the configured timeout window.
distractor_rationales: Certificate expiry fails handshakes with a different error, not intermittent 504s.
Malformed headers produce 4xx responses from the target path, not a load balancer 504.
Blocked health checks mark targets unhealthy, contradicting the healthy status.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options describe handshake failures, target rejections, or failed health checks instead of slow target responses.

questions.subdomain: 4.3 Optimize applications by using AWS services and features
questions.question: A stream serves eight consumer applications. One lagging consumer's re-reading slows the others, and the finance-reporting consumer needs single-digit-millisecond reads on its own dedicated capacity. Which consumer mechanism fits?
options: Enhanced fan-out, which gives each registered consumer its own dedicated pipe and read throughput.
Adding more shards so every consumer shares the enlarged capacity evenly.
Converting the stream to a standard SQS queue with eight consumers.
Having the lagging consumer read less frequently so the shared throughput opens up for the others.
questions.correct_rationale: Enhanced fan-out registers each consumer with dedicated throughput, isolating a lagging consumer's reads from the others.
distractor_rationales: More shards add capacity but consumers still contend on the shared retrieval model.
An SQS queue delivers each message once, which eight consumers cannot each independently read.
Reading less often does not create isolation; it delays that consumer further.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options scale the shared pipe, switch to a once-only queue, or throttle a consumer instead of isolating delivery.

questions.subdomain: 4.1 Assist in a root cause analysis
questions.question: An auditor asks who deleted a production security group, when, and from where. Which AWS record answers this?
options: The security team's incident ticket queue, where human reports about the deletion arrive after the fact.
The application's debug logs from the Region where the deleted resource lived.
CloudTrail event history, which records account API activity including the caller, time, and source.
The VPC flow logs captured for the deleted security group's subnets and interfaces.
questions.correct_rationale: CloudTrail records API activity with the caller identity, time, and source, which is exactly the audit question.
distractor_rationales: Tickets record human process, not the API call evidence.
Application logs describe app behavior, not account API actions.
Flow logs capture network traffic, not control-plane API calls.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options look at app logs, process tickets, or network flows instead of the API audit record.

questions.subdomain: 4.2 Apply logging, monitoring, and observability best practices
questions.question: A compliance review needs a record of every API Gateway request: caller IP, path, response latency, and status, captured at the API layer with no application changes. Which mechanism records it?
options: X-Ray traces sampled at a low rate for latency analysis of a fraction of calls.
The Lambda function's own structured logs, written by the handler for the requests it happens to see.
API Gateway execution logging delivered into CloudWatch Logs for the stage.
The load balancer's access logs covering the API's backend fleet instead of the API itself.
questions.correct_rationale: Execution logging at the API Gateway stage records each request's details into CloudWatch Logs without touching application code.
distractor_rationales: Sampled traces give latency for a subset, not a complete request record.
Handler logs capture only what the function logs and miss requests rejected before invocation.
Backend access logs miss everything the API layer handles itself.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options log inside the function, sample, or capture the wrong layer.

questions.subdomain: 4.2 Apply logging, monitoring, and observability best practices
questions.question: Operations must be paged when an application load balancer starts returning elevated 5xx counts to users. The load balancer's metrics already flow into CloudWatch. Which mechanism pages them?
options: Raising the targets' health-check thresholds so that the failing period looks much healthier on paper.
A daily export of the load balancer's metrics into a spreadsheet that an analyst reviews the next morning.
A weekly meeting where the team reviews the load balancer's dashboards together.
A CloudWatch alarm on the load balancer's 5xx-count metric notifying an SNS paging topic.
questions.correct_rationale: An alarm on the published 5xx metric pages through SNS as soon as the count crosses the threshold.
distractor_rationales: Hiding errors by tuning health checks does not page anyone and worsens routing.
A daily spreadsheet review is not paging within minutes.
A weekly review is slower still.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options review later, meet, or mask the signal instead of alarming on it.

docLinks.title: CloudWatch metrics for application load balancers

questions.subdomain: 4.3 Optimize applications by using AWS services and features
questions.question: A reporting team's heavy analytical queries slow the transactional application sharing the same RDS instance. Reports tolerate data that is minutes behind. Which change offloads the report load?
options: Migrating the reports to run inside the application's request path during business hours.
A larger instance class for the shared primary instance, sized for the report peaks.
A read replica that serves the reporting queries while replicating from the primary.
Taking the production database offline each night while the reports run their queries.
questions.correct_rationale: A read replica serves analytical reads from a copy that trails the primary, isolating report load from transactional traffic.
distractor_rationales: Running reports inside the request path worsens the interference.
A larger primary still shares every query path between analysts and transactions.
Nightly outages trade availability for reports, which no one asked for.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options resize the shared instance, worsen interference, or take the database offline.

docLinks.title: Working with DB instance read replicas

questions.subdomain: 4.1 Assist in a root cause analysis
questions.question: A trace shows the function's segment taking 800 milliseconds, but the time inside an external HTTP call the function makes is invisible in the segment detail. Which X-Ray construct records that inner work separately?
options: A CloudWatch metric emitted for the external call's duration alongside the traces.
A brand-new trace started inside the function for every external call it makes.
A subsegment, which records the inner work of calls to external services.
A metadata field on the segment that merely notes the external call happened.
questions.correct_rationale: Subsegments record granular work inside a segment, including downstream HTTP calls, making the inner duration visible in trace detail.
distractor_rationales: A metric shows duration distribution but not where in this trace the time went.
A separate trace breaks the single request path the team is reading.
A metadata note records a string; it does not time or display the call.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options fork the trace, aggregate into metrics, or annotate instead of instrumenting.

questions.subdomain: 4.3 Optimize applications by using AWS services and features
questions.question: An API's catalog endpoint is called thousands of times a minute from users worldwide, and each call makes the backend compute the same response for minutes at a time. Latency from distant Regions is the complaint. Which change serves those responses from closer to the users?
options: Increase the backend's instance size so that each computed response returns somewhat faster.
Move the backend's compute into every Region the users call from and run it everywhere.
Replicate the response database into each user's nearest Region and keep every copy in sync.
Configure CloudFront to cache the endpoint's responses at edge locations near the users.
questions.correct_rationale: CloudFront caches responses at edge locations near users, serving repeats without crossing back to the origin for the cache duration.
distractor_rationales: Faster computation shortens each response but every distant user still crosses the same distance.
Multi-Region compute multiplies the backend everywhere instead of reusing each computed response.
Database replication still runs the backend compute per request and adds data-consistency work.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options multiply compute or data, or speed the origin without shortening the distance.

docLinks.title: Control the cache key with a policy

questions.subdomain: 1.1 Develop code for applications that are hosted on AWS
questions.question: A team is building a shared task board where many users edit the same list through a GraphQL API backed by a DynamoDB table. Every open client must have other users' edits pushed to it over a persistent connection rather than polling for changes. The push must be produced by the GraphQL write operation itself, with no separate publishing code written by the team. Which design meets these requirements?
options: Expose the edits as AppSync mutations and have clients subscribe to them so each mutation reaches subscribers.
Run an API Gateway WebSocket API whose Lambda code writes each edit and then posts it to every connection ID.
Expose the edits as AppSync mutations and have clients re-run a list query every few seconds to pick up changes.
Store the edits in an S3 object per board and have clients download the object again when the user taps refresh.
questions.correct_rationale: AppSync subscriptions are invoked by mutations and push the mutation's selection set to connected subscribers, so no publish code is needed.
distractor_rationales: A WebSocket API pushes over a persistent connection, but the team must write and maintain the code that posts to each connection.
Mutations satisfy the write side, but re-running a query on a timer is polling, which the push requirement rules out.
Downloading an object on refresh is neither a push over a persistent connection nor tied to the write operation.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options push with custom publishing code, poll instead of pushing, or do neither.

questions.subdomain: 1.1 Develop code for applications that are hosted on AWS
questions.question: An order service publishes price-change events that three downstream services consume from their own queues. Each downstream service must process the events for a given product in exactly the order they were published. One publish call from the order service must deliver the event to all three services rather than three separate sends. Which messaging design meets these requirements?
options: Write the events to a DynamoDB table and have each service scan the table on a schedule for new rows to process.
Send each event three times from the order service, once to each service's SQS FIFO queue with the product ID as the group.
Publish to an SNS FIFO topic with the product ID as the message group, and subscribe three SQS FIFO queues to it.
Publish to an SNS standard topic and subscribe three SQS standard queues, one per downstream service.
questions.correct_rationale: An SNS FIFO topic fans one publish out to subscribed SQS FIFO queues while keeping strict ordering and deduplication per message group.
distractor_rationales: Scheduled scans neither preserve publish order per product nor deliver from a single publish operation.
Three FIFO queues give per-product ordering, but the service makes three sends, which the single-publish requirement rules out.
A standard topic fans out from one publish, but standard topics and queues do not guarantee strict ordering.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options keep order with three separate sends, fan out without ordering, or do neither.

questions.subdomain: 1.1 Develop code for applications that are hosted on AWS
questions.question: A clickstream is delivered to an S3 data lake through Amazon Data Firehose. Each record must have internal user IDs replaced by hashed values before it is written to the destination. What should the developer configure?
options: Turn on Firehose data transformation with a Lambda function that hashes the IDs in each incoming record.
Configure the producers to send records to an SQS queue first and drop any record that contains an ID.
Run a nightly job that reads the written S3 objects, hashes the IDs, and overwrites the objects afterward.
Add an S3 lifecycle rule on the destination bucket that rewrites the user ID fields as objects age.
questions.correct_rationale: Firehose can invoke a Lambda function to transform incoming records before it delivers them to the destination.
distractor_rationales: Dropping records loses data instead of transforming it, and adds a queue Firehose does not need.
A nightly rewrite lets unhashed IDs land in the destination first, which the requirement forbids.
Lifecycle rules transition or expire objects; they do not rewrite field contents.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options transform after delivery, misuse lifecycle rules, or discard the records.

docLinks.title: Transform source data in Amazon Data Firehose

questions.subdomain: 1.1 Develop code for applications that are hosted on AWS
questions.question: A batch importer uses the AWS SDK to write to a DynamoDB table, and bursts of writes are being throttled. The fix must live in the SDK client configuration rather than in hand-written retry loops in the importer. The client must also slow the first attempt of new requests when throttling is detected, not just its retries. Which change meets these requirements?
options: Raise the client's connection timeout so throttled writes wait longer before the request is abandoned.
Wrap each write in importer code that sleeps before every new request after any throttling error is caught.
Set the SDK retry mode to standard so throttled requests are retried with backoff by the client itself.
Set the SDK retry mode to adaptive, which adds a client-side rate limiter on top of standard retries.
questions.correct_rationale: Adaptive mode includes standard mode retries plus a client-side rate limiter that can delay initial requests when throttling is detected.
distractor_rationales: A longer connection timeout does not reduce the request rate or retry throttled writes.
Hand-written sleeps can delay new requests, but the fix must be client configuration, not importer code.
Standard mode is SDK configuration, but it backs off retries and does not delay the initial request.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options retry without rate limiting, rate-limit in custom code, or change an unrelated timeout.

questions.subdomain: 1.1 Develop code for applications that are hosted on AWS
questions.question: A support portal uses Amazon Translate to localize help articles. Product names keep being translated into ordinary words, and the brand team wants each product name kept or rendered exactly as they specify. What should the developer use?
options: Create a custom terminology that lists each product name and its required form, and pass it with requests.
Raise the formality setting on each request so product names are treated as formal proper nouns.
Translate each article twice and keep the output whose product names look closer to the source text.
Replace product names with random tokens before translation and hope the tokens pass through untouched.
questions.correct_rationale: Custom terminologies supplied with translation requests make brand and product names translate to the desired result.
distractor_rationales: Formality changes register, not how specific names are rendered.
Running the same translation twice does not control how names are translated.
Untracked random tokens give no defined mapping back and are not a supported way to fix names.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options change tone, repeat translation, or use an unsupported workaround.

questions.subdomain: 1.2 Develop code for AWS Lambda
questions.question: A Lambda function is being extended with new integrations. The function must reach an RDS database in private subnets of a VPC without exposing that database to the internet. The function must also call a third-party payment API on the public internet. How should the function's networking be configured?
options: Attach the function to the database's private subnets with no route to the internet from those subnets.
Attach the function to private subnets that route internet traffic to a NAT gateway in a public subnet.
Attach the function to a public subnet with an internet gateway route and rely on that subnet for outbound calls.
Run the function outside any VPC so it reaches the internet through Lambda's default networking.
questions.correct_rationale: Private subnets keep database access internal, and a NAT gateway in a public subnet gives the private subnet outbound internet access.
distractor_rationales: Private subnets reach the database, but with no internet route the payment API call fails.
A Lambda function in a public subnet does not get a public IP, so the internet gateway route alone does not give it access.
Outside the VPC the function can reach the internet but cannot reach the database in private subnets.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options reach the database but not the internet, the internet but not the database, or neither.

docLinks.title: Enable internet access for VPC-connected Lambda functions

questions.subdomain: 1.2 Develop code for AWS Lambda
questions.question: A high-traffic Lambda function reads the same Parameter Store values on every invocation. Invocations should stop calling Parameter Store each time and instead reuse values retrieved earlier. The team wants an AWS-provided component for this rather than writing and maintaining their own caching code. What should the developer do?
options: Add the AWS Parameters and Secrets Lambda Extension and read parameters from its local endpoint.
Write a module-level dictionary in the handler code that stores each parameter after the first lookup.
Use the AWS SDK's Parameter Store client and call it at the start of each invocation for fresh values.
Copy every parameter value into the deployment package so the code reads values from a bundled file.
questions.correct_rationale: The extension retrieves parameter values and caches them, so later reads come from the cache instead of Parameter Store.
distractor_rationales: A hand-written cache avoids repeat calls, but it is custom code the team wanted to avoid.
The SDK client is AWS-provided, but calling it each invocation is the repeated lookup the team wants to stop.
Bundling values removes Parameter Store from the design, so updated values need a redeploy.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options cache with custom code, keep calling every time, or stop using Parameter Store.

docLinks.title: Using Parameter Store parameters in Lambda functions

questions.subdomain: 1.2 Develop code for AWS Lambda
questions.question: Several Lambda functions process large media files through libraries that expect normal file paths. All of the functions must read and write the same set of files concurrently through a local directory. Files written by one invocation must stay available to later invocations after it ends. Which storage option meets these requirements?
options: Store each file as an S3 object and download it to the function's /tmp directory at the start of each run.
Connect the functions to the VPC and mount a shared Amazon EFS file system at a local path in each.
Mount a shared in-memory directory between functions by placing them all behind the same Lambda alias.
Increase each function's ephemeral storage and write every file to its own /tmp directory for later use.
questions.correct_rationale: Lambda can mount an EFS file system to a local directory over the VPC network, giving shared and persistent file access.
distractor_rationales: S3 keeps files after the run, but downloading copies to /tmp is not concurrent shared access through a local directory.
Aliases route invocations to versions; they do not create a shared directory between functions.
Ephemeral storage is per execution environment, so it is neither shared across functions nor durable.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options assume an alias shares memory, copy files instead of sharing a directory, or use per-instance storage.

docLinks.title: Configuring Amazon EFS file system access for Lambda functions

questions.subdomain: 1.2 Develop code for AWS Lambda
questions.question: A Lambda function consumes a Kinesis data stream, and one malformed record makes the whole batch fail and retry. The function must tell Lambda which record failed so earlier successful records are not processed again. Lambda must also split the failing batch so the bad record is isolated and retried in smaller batches. Which event source mapping settings meet these requirements?
options: Turn on ReportBatchItemFailures and BisectBatchOnFunctionError, and return the failed record's sequence number.
Reduce the stream's retention period so failing records age out of the stream before they are retried again.
Turn on ReportBatchItemFailures and return the failed sequence number, with batch splitting left turned off.
Turn on BisectBatchOnFunctionError and raise an error for the whole batch without returning sequence numbers.
questions.correct_rationale: With both settings on, Lambda bisects the batch at the returned sequence number and retries only the remaining records.
distractor_rationales: Shortening retention discards data and does not tell Lambda which record failed.
Reporting item failures avoids reprocessing earlier records, but the batch is not split to isolate the bad record.
Bisecting splits failing batches, but without reported failures earlier successful records are processed again.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options report without splitting, split without reporting, or drop data through retention.

docLinks.title: Configuring partial batch response with Kinesis Data Streams and Lambda

questions.subdomain: 1.2 Develop code for AWS Lambda
questions.question: A Lambda function processes a Kinesis stream, and records that exhaust their retries are lost today. Only records from invocations that exhausted their retries must be retained, captured by Lambda itself rather than by handler code. Each retained document must contain the original record payload itself, not only the shard ID and sequence-number range, because the stream may have expired before anyone investigates. Which configuration meets these requirements?
options: Raise the event source mapping batch size so fewer invocations happen and fewer records reach the retry limit.
Log the full event payload to CloudWatch Logs inside the handler before the function starts processing.
Add an S3 bucket as the on-failure destination on the function's Kinesis event source mapping.
Add an SQS queue as the on-failure destination on the mapping, which queues each failed batch's shard ID and sequence range.
questions.correct_rationale: An on-failure destination on the mapping retains failed invocation records, and for S3 destinations Lambda sends the entire invocation record with metadata.
distractor_rationales: Larger batches do not retain failed records and can make each failure affect more records.
Logging every payload records data, but it is not a retention mechanism tied to failed invocations.
An SQS on-failure destination is captured by Lambda, but it receives only metadata such as the shard ID and sequence-number range, not the original record payload.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options keep metadata without the full record, log everything regardless of failure, or tune batching.

docLinks.title: Retaining discarded records from a Kinesis event source

questions.subdomain: 1.3 Use data stores during application development
questions.question: A product catalog stored in RDS sits behind an ElastiCache cluster. Readers must see a product's new price from the cache right after the price is written, with no stale period. Cached entries for products that nobody reads should not occupy the cache indefinitely. Which caching approach meets these requirements?
options: Load items into the cache on a miss and set a TTL, leaving the cache untouched when prices are written.
Write each change to the database and the cache together, with entries stored without any expiration set.
Write each change to the database and the cache together, with a TTL so unread entries expire.
Read prices straight from the database replica and disable the cache cluster to avoid serving stale data.
questions.correct_rationale: Write-through updates the cache whenever the database is written, and a TTL removes the superfluous entries write-through can add.
distractor_rationales: Lazy loading with a TTL limits idle entries, but readers can see the old price until the entry expires.
Write-through keeps reads fresh, but without a TTL entries that nobody reads stay in the cache.
Dropping the cache avoids staleness but abandons the caching layer the design is built on.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options keep the cache fresh but full, keep it lean but stale, or remove it.

docLinks.title: Caching strategies for Memcached and Valkey or Redis OSS

questions.subdomain: 1.3 Use data stores during application development
questions.question: A microservice stores user session carts and needs low-latency reads. Acknowledged cart writes must not be lost when nodes fail, so the store itself must be durable across Availability Zones. The team wants to keep using Redis-compatible data structures and client libraries in the code. Which data store meets these requirements?
options: An ElastiCache for Redis OSS cluster used as the sole store for the carts, with no durable database behind it.
An RDS for MySQL database with the carts stored as JSON columns and read through an ORM layer.
Amazon MemoryDB used as the primary database for the carts, with Multi-AZ durability built in.
Amazon DynamoDB as the primary store, accessed through its own SDK in place of the Redis clients.
questions.correct_rationale: MemoryDB delivers in-memory performance with Multi-AZ durability and can serve as the primary database.
distractor_rationales: ElastiCache keeps the Redis clients, but as the sole store it is a cache and does not give the durable, Multi-AZ primary storage the carts need.
RDS is durable but neither Redis-compatible nor an in-memory store.
DynamoDB is durable across AZs, but it drops the Redis-compatible structures and clients the team wants.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options are durable but not Redis-compatible, compatible but not durable, or neither.

questions.subdomain: 1.3 Use data stores during application development
questions.question: A team runs a self-managed MongoDB cluster and wants a managed AWS database. They want to keep their existing application code and MongoDB drivers. Which service fits?
options: Amazon DocumentDB, which works with the same application code, drivers, and tools used with MongoDB.
Amazon DynamoDB, after rewriting every query to use the DynamoDB SDK and its own data model.
Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, after converting each document collection into relational tables.
Amazon Neptune, after remodeling the documents as graph vertices and edges for the same queries.
questions.correct_rationale: DocumentDB lets teams use the same application code, drivers, and tools they use with MongoDB.
distractor_rationales: DynamoDB needs a rewrite to its own API, which the team wants to avoid.
A relational conversion changes the data model and the code.
A graph database needs a new data model and query language.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options all force a rewrite of the data model or the code.

questions.subdomain: 1.3 Use data stores during application development
questions.question: A storefront keeps products in DynamoDB keyed by product ID. Shoppers must find products by typing free-text words that can appear anywhere in titles and descriptions. The team wants a managed search and analytics engine rather than search logic they write themselves. What should the developer add?
options: Put CloudFront in front of the product API so repeated searches are cached at edge locations.
Add a DynamoDB global secondary index keyed on product title to look up exact title values.
Scan the DynamoDB table and filter descriptions with application code that matches each typed word.
Index the product documents in an Amazon OpenSearch Service domain and send shopper queries to it.
questions.correct_rationale: OpenSearch is a managed open-source search and analytics engine suited to free-text search over documents.
distractor_rationales: Caching repeats responses but adds no ability to search text.
A GSI is managed, but it supports key lookups on whole values, not free-text matching inside text.
Scanning with custom matching finds words, but it is self-written search logic and scales poorly.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options search with custom code, index exact keys, or only cache.

questions.subdomain: 1.3 Use data stores during application development
questions.question: An internal booking app needs a MySQL-compatible relational database with transactions. Traffic is quiet most of the day but spikes sharply at unpredictable times. Capacity must grow to meet those spikes and shrink afterward without the team resizing instances. Which database option fits?
options: An Aurora cluster that the team resizes with a scheduled script at the same times each morning and evening.
A DynamoDB table in on-demand mode with the booking logic moved into application-side transactions.
A provisioned Aurora cluster sized for the highest spike seen so far, left at that size all day.
Amazon Aurora Serverless v2, which scales capacity to the peak load and back down when the surge ends.
questions.correct_rationale: Aurora Serverless scales capacity automatically for peak load and scales back down when activity drops.
distractor_rationales: Scheduled resizing is manual effort and misses spikes that come at unpredictable times.
DynamoDB is not MySQL-compatible, which the app requires.
Sizing for the peak handles spikes, but capacity never shrinks afterward.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options overprovision, resize on a fixed schedule, or change the database engine.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Implement authentication and authorization mechanisms for applications and AWS services
questions.question: Developers sign in to the company's IAM Identity Center portal and also run AWS CLI commands from laptops. No long-term access keys may be stored on any laptop. Developers should not have to re-enter credentials every time the CLI's short-term credentials expire during a session. How should the CLI be configured?
options: Share one IAM role's credentials with the team through a chat channel that is refreshed each morning.
Create an IAM user per developer with access keys in the CLI config file that do not expire on a schedule.
Have developers copy temporary credentials from the portal into the CLI config file each time they expire.
Set up CLI profiles with IAM Identity Center so the CLI refreshes short-term credentials for the session.
questions.correct_rationale: With IAM Identity Center configured, the CLI renews expired AWS credentials as long as the sign-in session's cached credentials are valid.
distractor_rationales: Sharing credentials in chat breaks individual identity and still needs manual refresh.
Long-lived keys avoid re-entering credentials, but they are the long-term keys the policy forbids.
Copied temporary credentials avoid long-term keys, but developers must paste new ones each time they expire.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options repaste credentials, store long-term keys, or share credentials.

docLinks.title: Configuring IAM Identity Center authentication with the AWS CLI

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Implement authentication and authorization mechanisms for applications and AWS services
questions.question: A document-sharing app authenticates users and must decide whether a user can view, edit, or share each document. Authorization rules must be kept out of application code so they can change without redeploying the services. Security reviewers want those rules written in a policy language and managed in one central place. Which approach meets these requirements?
options: Write the rules as Cedar policies in one shared repository that is bundled into each service at build time.
Give every user an IAM user and attach IAM policies that name each document's object key individually.
Store the rules as Cedar policies in Amazon Verified Permissions and have services query it per decision.
Keep the rules as feature-flag values in AWS AppConfig that each service reads and interprets in its own code.
questions.correct_rationale: Verified Permissions externalizes authorization and centralizes policy management, with policies written in Cedar.
distractor_rationales: Cedar is a policy language kept in one place, but bundling it into every service means each rule change needs a redeployment.
IAM users per app user do not scale and are not meant for application end users.
AppConfig moves the values out of the code, but the rules are not written in a policy language or evaluated by a central policy engine.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options externalize without a policy engine, keep rules in code, or misuse IAM.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Implement authentication and authorization mechanisms for applications and AWS services
questions.question: An on-premises batch server must upload reports to an S3 bucket. The server must not hold long-term AWS access keys. It must authenticate with X.509 certificates already issued by the company's own certificate authority. How should the server obtain AWS credentials?
options: Register the CA as a trust anchor in IAM Roles Anywhere and exchange the server's certificate for temporary credentials.
Store the CA-issued certificate on the server next to an IAM user's access keys used for the uploads.
Have an operator assume a role in the console each day and paste the temporary credentials onto the server.
Make the bucket writable by anyone and rely on obscure object names to keep other uploads out.
questions.correct_rationale: Roles Anywhere lets workloads outside AWS authenticate with certificates from a trusted CA and receive temporary credentials.
distractor_rationales: The certificate is present, but the uploads still rely on long-term IAM user keys.
Pasted temporary credentials avoid long-term keys, but the server never authenticates with its certificate.
A public bucket removes authentication entirely.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options skip certificate authentication, keep long-term keys, or drop authentication.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Implement authentication and authorization mechanisms for applications and AWS services
questions.question: A company runs dozens of developer sandbox accounts under one organization. No IAM principal in any sandbox account, including account administrators, may disable CloudTrail. The control must be set once centrally rather than maintained separately inside each account. Which control meets these requirements?
options: Attach a service control policy to the sandbox OU that denies the CloudTrail stop and delete actions.
Turn on MFA for every sandbox user so that disabling CloudTrail requires a second sign-in factor first.
Add an IAM policy that denies the CloudTrail actions to every role in each account, managed account by account.
Create one central CloudWatch dashboard that shows CloudTrail status for all accounts in the organization.
questions.correct_rationale: SCPs centrally set the maximum available permissions for IAM users and roles across the organization's accounts.
distractor_rationales: MFA adds a sign-in factor but does not stop an authorized admin from disabling the trail.
Per-account deny policies can block the actions, but they are maintained in each account and admins there could edit them.
A central dashboard observes status but does not prevent anyone from disabling CloudTrail.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options block per account, only observe centrally, or add authentication without restricting actions.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Implement authentication and authorization mechanisms for applications and AWS services
questions.question: Developers share one SSH private key to reach Linux EC2 instances for debugging. Security wants SSH access granted through IAM policies so no shared keys are managed. What should the team use?
options: A new key pair per instance, with the private keys stored in a shared folder for the team.
EC2 Instance Connect, which controls SSH access with IAM policies and principals instead of shared keys.
Password authentication on each instance, with the password rotated by hand every month.
Security group rules that allow port 22 from the office network so any developer can connect.
questions.correct_rationale: EC2 Instance Connect uses IAM policies and principals to control SSH access, removing the need to share and manage SSH keys.
distractor_rationales: More key pairs still means managing and sharing keys.
Shared passwords replace one shared secret with another and bypass IAM.
Security groups control network reachability, not who is authorized.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options keep shared secrets or control the network instead of identity.

questions.subdomain: 2.2 Implement encryption and manage sensitive data by using AWS services
questions.question: A service in account B must read a database secret stored in Secrets Manager in account A. Account B's role must be granted access through the secret's resource policy. The secret must be encrypted so that account B can decrypt it. Which setup meets these requirements?
options: Keep the secret encrypted with the aws/secretsmanager key and grant account B's role in the secret's resource policy.
Encrypt the secret with a customer managed key whose policy allows account B, and grant B in the secret's policy.
Encrypt with a customer managed key that allows account B, and copy the secret's value into account B by hand.
Store the secret as a plaintext tag on the database instance so account B can read it through the API.
questions.correct_rationale: Cross-account access needs a customer managed key with a key policy for the other account, because the AWS managed key cannot be used cross-account.
distractor_rationales: The resource policy grants access, but the AWS managed key cannot be used for cross-account access, so decryption fails.
A shareable key is chosen, but copying the value by hand skips the secret's resource policy and breaks rotation.
A plaintext tag exposes the credential and is not encryption.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options grant access with an unusable key, copy the value by hand, or expose it in plaintext.

docLinks.title: Access AWS Secrets Manager secrets from a different account

questions.subdomain: 2.2 Implement encryption and manage sensitive data by using AWS services
questions.question: An app stores customer records in DynamoDB. Selected fields such as tax IDs must be encrypted by the app before the item ever leaves it. Readers must also be able to detect if any of the item's signed fields were changed after they were written. Which approach meets these requirements?
options: Store tax IDs in a separate table with a stricter IAM policy, neither encrypted nor signed by the app.
Use the AWS Database Encryption SDK and choose which fields are encrypted and which are signed.
Encrypt the tax ID with a direct KMS Encrypt call in the app, then store the ciphertext in the item.
Compute an HMAC over the item's attributes in the app so changes are detected, keeping tax IDs in plaintext.
questions.correct_rationale: The Database Encryption SDK adds client-side encryption and lets you choose the fields that are encrypted and the fields included in signatures.
distractor_rationales: A separate table with IAM limits access but neither encrypts nor signs.
Direct KMS encryption protects the field client-side, but it adds no signature to detect changes to other fields.
An HMAC lets readers detect changes, but the tax IDs leave the app unencrypted.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options encrypt without signing, encrypt server-side, or leave data in plaintext.

docLinks.title: What is the AWS Database Encryption SDK?

questions.subdomain: 2.2 Implement encryption and manage sensitive data by using AWS services
questions.question: Lambda functions in private subnets with no NAT gateway use secrets that are stored in Secrets Manager. The calls must not traverse the internet or use a NAT device. The functions must keep retrieving secrets at run time from Secrets Manager so rotated values are picked up. What should the developer configure?
options: Have the deployment pipeline resolve each secret and pass the values to the functions as encrypted environment variables.
Add a NAT gateway and package each secret value into the deployment artifact that the functions read at startup.
Create an interface VPC endpoint for Secrets Manager in the VPC and call the service through it.
Add a NAT gateway to the VPC and route the functions' Secrets Manager calls out through it.
questions.correct_rationale: Interface endpoints use AWS PrivateLink to reach Secrets Manager APIs privately without an internet gateway or NAT device.
distractor_rationales: No network path is needed at run time, but the values are fixed at deployment, so rotated secrets are not picked up.
A NAT gateway breaks the no-NAT rule, and packaged values are not retrieved at run time, so rotations are missed.
A NAT gateway lets the calls succeed at run time, but it uses the NAT device the rule forbids.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options freeze values at deploy time, use a NAT device, or use the wrong endpoint type.

docLinks.title: Using a Secrets Manager VPC endpoint

questions.subdomain: 2.2 Implement encryption and manage sensitive data by using AWS services
questions.question: A telemetry service encrypts millions of small messages with the AWS Encryption SDK and a KMS key. KMS request volume and cost from generating a data key per message must come down. The team wants bounded reuse, with limits on how long and how much each data key is used. What should the developer do?
options: Turn on data key caching in the Encryption SDK and set its security thresholds for age and usage.
Switch every message to direct KMS Encrypt calls so no data keys are generated by the SDK.
Turn on data key caching but cap each cached key at one message, so a new key is still requested per message.
Generate one data key at startup and reuse it for all messages, with no limit on its age or use.
questions.correct_rationale: Data key caching reuses cached data keys to cut KMS calls, and its security thresholds limit how much caching is used.
distractor_rationales: Direct KMS calls per message increase KMS requests and size limits apply.
Sending fewer messages changes the workload instead of the encryption design.
One long-lived key cuts KMS calls, but reuse is unbounded, which the team wants to avoid.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options reuse keys without limits, shrink the workload, or call KMS more often.

questions.subdomain: 2.3 Identify and mitigate security risks associated with using and integrating AI services into application development
questions.question: A claims app running in private subnets sends customer documents to Amazon Bedrock for summarization. Prompt traffic containing customer data must not leave the AWS network over the public internet. The app must keep calling Bedrock's managed foundation models rather than hosting its own model. What should the developer configure?
options: Create an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon Bedrock so the app calls the models over AWS PrivateLink.
Strip all customer names from the prompts in the browser before they reach the claims app.
Download an open-weight model and host it on EC2 instances inside the same private subnets as the app.
Route the app's Bedrock calls through a NAT gateway and rely on TLS to protect the prompt traffic.
questions.correct_rationale: AWS PrivateLink creates a private connection between the VPC and Bedrock, keeping traffic off the internet.
distractor_rationales: Client-side name stripping does not address the network path and misses other customer data.
Self-hosting keeps traffic local, but it abandons the managed Bedrock models the app must use.
TLS encrypts the traffic, but a NAT path still sends it to the public endpoint over the internet.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options self-host, use the public path, or redact without fixing the network path.

questions.subdomain: 2.3 Identify and mitigate security risks associated with using and integrating AI services into application development
questions.question: A benefits chatbot answers employee questions from retrieved policy passages using a Bedrock model. Answers that are not supported by the retrieved passages must be detected and blocked before reaching employees. The check must be a managed safeguard applied to model responses rather than custom scoring code. Which control meets these requirements?
options: Apply a Bedrock guardrail with denied topics for subjects unrelated to benefits and employee policies.
Lower the model's temperature to zero so that it repeats the retrieved passages more closely in answers.
Use a Bedrock guardrail's contextual grounding check with the retrieved passages as the reference source.
Write a Lambda function that compares each answer's words with the passages and blocks low-overlap answers.
questions.correct_rationale: Contextual grounding checks detect and filter hallucinations in responses when a reference source and query are provided.
distractor_rationales: Denied topics are a managed guardrail, but they block subjects, not answers unsupported by the passages.
Lower temperature reduces randomness but does not detect or block unsupported answers.
Custom overlap scoring targets unsupported answers, but it is self-written code rather than a managed safeguard.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options check grounding with custom code, filter topics instead, or only tune sampling.

docLinks.title: Use contextual grounding check to filter hallucinations in responses

questions.subdomain: 2.3 Identify and mitigate security risks associated with using and integrating AI services into application development
questions.question: A community app lets users chat with each other and with a generative AI assistant. Toxic content must be flagged both in user messages and in the assistant's generated replies. The team wants a managed NLP API for the detection rather than training and hosting its own classifier. Which approach meets these requirements?
options: Use Amazon Comprehend to detect the dominant language of each message and drop non-English text.
Send user messages and assistant replies to Amazon Comprehend toxicity detection and act on the results.
Send user messages to Comprehend toxicity detection and pass assistant replies through without any check.
Train a toxicity classifier on past chats, host it on an endpoint, and score messages and replies with it.
questions.correct_rationale: Comprehend toxicity detection can moderate peer-to-peer conversations and monitor generative AI inputs and outputs.
distractor_rationales: Language detection does not measure toxicity.
Comprehend is managed, but skipping the assistant's replies misses toxic generated output.
A custom classifier can cover both directions, but the team wanted a managed API, not a model to train and host.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options self-host a model, check one direction, or detect the wrong property.

questions.subdomain: 2.3 Identify and mitigate security risks associated with using and integrating AI services into application development
questions.question: A team will load thousands of S3 documents into a Bedrock knowledge base for an internal assistant. Before ingestion, they must find which objects contain sensitive data such as personal identifiers. The discovery must run as a managed scan of the S3 objects with findings, not as code the team writes. What should the developer use?
options: Enable S3 default encryption on the bucket so that sensitive objects are protected before ingestion.
Ingest everything first and then add a guardrail that blocks personal data from appearing in answers.
Write a Lambda function with regular expressions that scans each object and tags matches before ingestion.
Run Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery on the source bucket and review its findings before ingestion.
questions.correct_rationale: Macie generates a finding when it detects sensitive data in an S3 object, identifying objects to exclude or clean.
distractor_rationales: Encryption protects data at rest but does not identify which objects hold sensitive data.
A guardrail is managed, but it acts after ingestion instead of finding sensitive objects beforehand.
Regex scanning finds some identifiers, but it is custom code rather than a managed discovery service.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options scan with custom code, act after ingestion, or encrypt without discovering.

questions.subdomain: 3.1 Prepare application artifacts to be deployed to AWS
questions.question: Build jobs pull public base images from Docker Hub and sometimes fail when the upstream registry is slow. Builds must pull those images through the team's ECR private registry URI. ECR must keep the cached images in sync with the upstream registry rather than the team copying them by hand. What should the developer configure?
options: Point the builds at Docker Hub directly and add retries with longer timeouts to the build scripts.
Turn on ECR scan on push so that slow or failing base images are flagged in the build reports.
Pull each base image locally, retag it, and push it to an ECR private repository when someone remembers.
Create an ECR pull through cache rule for Docker Hub, with credentials in a Secrets Manager secret.
questions.correct_rationale: Pull through cache rules sync an upstream registry with the private registry, and authenticated upstreams use a Secrets Manager secret.
distractor_rationales: Retries keep the upstream source but still depend on Docker Hub and do not use the ECR URI.
Scanning checks vulnerabilities; it does not cache or sync images.
Manual pushes put images behind the ECR URI, but nothing keeps them in sync with upstream.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options copy by hand, keep pulling upstream, or scan instead of caching.

docLinks.title: Sync an upstream registry with an Amazon ECR private registry

questions.subdomain: 3.1 Prepare application artifacts to be deployed to AWS
questions.question: An ECS service needs a database password that is stored in Secrets Manager. The password must reach the container as an environment variable without appearing in the task definition. ECS must be able to fetch the secret when it starts each task. How should the task definition be prepared?
options: Give the task execution role permission to read the secret and paste the password into the environment field.
Reference the secret ARN in the container's secrets field and give the task execution role permission to read it.
Bake the password into the container image at build time and rotate it by rebuilding the image monthly.
Reference the secret ARN in the container's secrets field and grant read permission to the application's task role.
questions.correct_rationale: The secrets field injects the value as an environment variable, and the task execution role needs Secrets Manager permissions.
distractor_rationales: The role can read the secret, but pasting the value into the environment field exposes it in the task definition.
Baking a password into an image exposes it to anyone who can pull the image.
The secrets field keeps the value out of the definition, but ECS fetches it with the task execution role, not the task role, so the task cannot start.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options grant the wrong role, expose the value, or bake it into the image.

docLinks.title: Pass Secrets Manager secrets through Amazon ECS environment variables

questions.subdomain: 3.1 Prepare application artifacts to be deployed to AWS
questions.question: A team deploys a web app to Elastic Beanstalk and wants environment settings and extra resources defined in files kept with the app's source code. Where should these files go?
options: In a README file in the bundle that the operations team follows by hand after each deployment.
In a Dockerfile placed beside the code, which Elastic Beanstalk reads for every platform type.
In YAML or JSON .config files inside an .ebextensions folder at the root of the source bundle.
In environment variables typed into the console after each new environment is created by hand.
questions.correct_rationale: Configuration files with a .config extension in an .ebextensions folder of the source bundle configure the environment and its resources.
distractor_rationales: Manual steps from a README are not applied by Elastic Beanstalk.
A Dockerfile applies to Docker platforms and is not the general configuration mechanism.
Console entries are not kept with the source code.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options use a platform-specific file, manual steps, or settings kept outside the code.

docLinks.title: Advanced environment customization with configuration files (.ebextensions)

questions.subdomain: 3.2 Implement and automate application testing in AWS environments
questions.question: A developer wants to invoke a Lambda function locally with a realistic S3 put event but does not want to write the event JSON by hand. Which AWS SAM CLI command helps?
options: sam build, which compiles the function and writes a sample event file into the build folder.
sam local generate-event, which produces sample event payloads for supported AWS services.
sam validate, which checks the template and prints an example event for each defined function.
sam deploy --guided, which uploads the function and records an event sample for local testing.
questions.correct_rationale: The sam local generate-event subcommand generates event payload samples for supported AWS services.
distractor_rationales: sam build prepares artifacts; it does not generate events.
sam validate checks template syntax; it does not output events.
sam deploy deploys the stack; it does not create local test events.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options build, deploy, or validate instead of generating events.

questions.subdomain: 3.2 Implement and automate application testing in AWS environments
questions.question: A front-end team hosts a web app on Amplify Hosting from a GitHub repository. Reviewers must test each proposed change on its own URL before it is merged into the main branch. Those test URLs and their temporary resources must be removed when the change is closed. What should the team turn on?
options: Amplify pull request previews, which deploy each PR to a preview URL that is deleted when it closes.
Branch auto-deletion for the main branch so that old builds of main are removed after each new merge.
A CloudFront distribution in front of production with a query string that hides unfinished features.
A second Amplify branch named staging that reviewers share and that the team cleans up by hand monthly.
questions.correct_rationale: Pull request previews deploy each PR to a unique preview URL, and the URL and temporary backend are deleted when the PR closes.
distractor_rationales: Cleaning up main's builds removes resources but gives no per-change test URL.
Hidden features in production are not isolated test environments.
A shared staging branch gives a test URL, but not one per change, and cleanup is manual.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options share one environment, clean up without previews, or test in production.

questions.subdomain: 3.2 Implement and automate application testing in AWS environments
questions.question: A team defines its infrastructure in AWS CDK with TypeScript and uses Jest for tests. A test must fail if a refactor changes a specific resource property, such as a queue's visibility timeout. The test must run against the synthesized template in CI without deploying anything to an account. Which approach meets these requirements?
options: Review cdk diff output by hand during code review and approve changes that look correct to reviewers.
Deploy the stack to a test account in CI and call the SQS API to read back the queue's attributes.
Write fine-grained CDK assertions tests that check that property in the synthesized template.
Run cdk synth in CI and check that the command exits successfully without inspecting the template.
questions.correct_rationale: Fine-grained assertions test specific properties of the generated CloudFormation template and detect regressions.
distractor_rationales: Manual diff review is not an automated test that fails on change.
Reading the deployed queue checks the property, but it deploys to an account, which the test must avoid.
Synthesis runs without deploying, but a successful exit does not check the property.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options deploy to check, synthesize without checking, or rely on manual review.

questions.subdomain: 3.2 Implement and automate application testing in AWS environments
questions.question: A team wants evidence about how its service behaves under stress. They must test whether it keeps serving traffic when one Availability Zone's instances stop, by injecting real faults into running resources. They want a managed service to define and run these experiments rather than custom scripts. What should the team use?
options: A managed load test from AWS Distributed Load Testing that sends heavy traffic while every zone stays healthy.
An architecture diagram review where the team traces each request path for single points of failure.
A cron script with admin credentials that terminates random instances using the EC2 API each week.
AWS Fault Injection Service, running an experiment that stops instances in one Availability Zone.
questions.correct_rationale: AWS FIS is a managed service for fault injection experiments on AWS workloads.
distractor_rationales: A managed load test exercises capacity but injects no faults into the resources.
A diagram review reasons about failures without testing them.
A script injects faults, but it is custom tooling rather than a managed experiment service.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options inject faults with custom scripts, test load without faults, or test nothing.
