questions.subdomain: 3.2 Implement and automate application testing in AWS environments
questions.question: A developer is changing the input and output processing of one Task state in a large Step Functions workflow. The developer must test that one state in isolation without creating or updating a state machine. The test must not call the real downstream service, so its response has to be mocked. Which approach meets these requirements?
options: Call the TestState API with the state's definition and an IAM role that lets it call the real service.
Start an execution of the production state machine with sample input and read the execution event history.
Call the TestState API with the state's definition and a mocked service response for the integration.
Deploy a copy of the whole workflow to a test account with the target function replaced by a stub.
questions.correct_rationale: TestState accepts a state definition and runs it without a state machine, and it can mock service integrations.
distractor_rationales: TestState isolates the state, but with a real role and no mock it calls the actual service.
A production execution neither isolates the state nor avoids the real service.
A stub avoids the real service, but it creates a whole state machine to test one state.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options isolate without mocking, mock by deploying a workflow, or test in production.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 Deploy code by using AWS continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) services
questions.question: An ECS service runs ten tasks and uses the rolling update deployment type. During a deployment the service must never drop below ten healthy tasks. ECS must be allowed to start replacement tasks before it stops old ones. How should the deployment configuration be set?
options: Scale the service to twenty tasks first, then deploy with minimumHealthyPercent 50 and maximumPercent 100.
Switch the service to the external deployment type and manage task replacement with a custom controller.
Set maximumPercent to 200 so new tasks start first, and leave minimumHealthyPercent at 50 for the service.
Set minimumHealthyPercent to 100 and maximumPercent to 200 on the service's deployment configuration.
questions.correct_rationale: minimumHealthyPercent sets the lower limit of healthy tasks, and maximumPercent above 100 lets replacements start first.
distractor_rationales: Pre-scaling keeps ten healthy tasks, but a 100 maximum makes ECS stop old tasks before it starts replacements.
An external controller abandons the managed rolling update for custom code.
A 200 maximum lets replacements start first, but a 50 minimum lets healthy tasks drop to five.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options stop tasks before replacing them, allow capacity to drop, or replace ECS with custom control.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 Deploy code by using AWS continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) services
questions.question: A V2 pipeline with a GitHub connection source deploys a library to production. Production releases must start when a Git tag matching release/v* is pushed. Ordinary pushes to feature branches must not start this pipeline. How should the pipeline trigger be configured?
options: Add a push trigger filter that excludes feature/** branches and includes every other branch name.
Add a push trigger filter on Git tags that includes the release/v* pattern for the source action.
Add push trigger filters that include the release/v* tag pattern and also include every branch with **.
Add a manual approval action at the start of the pipeline and reject runs that came from features.
questions.correct_rationale: Push triggers can filter on Git tags, so a tag include pattern starts the pipeline on matching tag pushes.
distractor_rationales: Excluding feature branches stops those runs, but it does not start releases on tags.
The tag filter starts releases on matching tags, but the ** branch filter also starts the pipeline on feature-branch pushes.
Rejecting runs by hand still starts them and wastes approval effort.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options ignore tags, filter branches without tags, or filter by hand.

docLinks.title: Filter triggers on code push or pull requests

questions.subdomain: 3.3 Deploy code by using AWS continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) services
questions.question: A CloudFormation stack contains an application tier and a production database. Stack updates must be prevented from accidentally replacing or deleting the database resource. The application tier's resources must remain updatable through normal stack updates. What should the developer set on the stack?
options: A stack policy with no Allow statements, so every resource in the stack is protected from updates by default.
Drift detection scheduled daily so that changes to the database are reported after each stack update.
An IAM policy for the deployment role that allows all CloudFormation actions on the stack's resources.
A stack policy that allows updates on all resources and adds a Deny statement for the database resource.
questions.correct_rationale: A stack policy controls update actions on designated resources, and a Deny statement protects the database while Allow covers the rest.
distractor_rationales: This protects the database, but with no Allow statement the application tier cannot be updated either.
Drift detection reports changes after the fact; it does not prevent them.
Broad IAM permissions allow other updates but do nothing to protect the database during updates.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options protect everything, protect nothing, or only report afterward.

questions.subdomain: 4.1 Assist in a root cause analysis
questions.question: New ECS tasks for a service keep stopping a few seconds after launch. The developer must find why the tasks stopped, not just that they stopped. The tasks stopped within the last hour, and the developer wants the reason from ECS itself rather than the application's own logs. What should the developer check first?
options: Check the service's running task count in the console to confirm how many tasks have stopped.
Increase the service's desired count so that more tasks are launched while the cause is investigated.
Describe the stopped tasks and read the stopCode and the container reason fields that ECS records.
Open the application's log group and search for errors written by the container before it exited.
questions.correct_rationale: Describing a stopped task returns a stopCode and container reason that explain why ECS stopped it.
distractor_rationales: The task count shows that tasks stop, not why.
More tasks repeat the failure without diagnosing it.
Application logs may explain some failures, but they are not the ECS-recorded reason and are empty if the container never started.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options use app logs, count tasks, or scale instead of reading ECS stop reasons.

questions.subdomain: 4.1 Assist in a root cause analysis
questions.question: An in-place CodeDeploy deployment to EC2 instances failed during a lifecycle script. The team wants to review the deployment log data from all instances in one place. What should they do?
options: Open the CodeDeploy console's application list and read the script output shown for each revision.
Turn on CloudTrail and read the CreateDeployment events to see each failed script's output lines.
Re-run the deployment with a larger instance type so the failing lifecycle script has more memory.
Install the CloudWatch agent to send CodeDeploy agent and deployment logs to CloudWatch Logs.
questions.correct_rationale: CodeDeploy log data can be viewed centrally by setting up the CloudWatch agent to send it to CloudWatch.
distractor_rationales: The application list does not hold the instances' script logs.
CloudTrail records API calls, not script output on the instances.
A larger instance is a guess, not a review of the logs.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options read API history, the wrong console page, or change the instance blindly.

docLinks.title: View log data for CodeDeploy EC2/On-Premises deployments

questions.subdomain: 4.1 Assist in a root cause analysis
questions.question: An application on EC2 intermittently cannot reach a database instance in another subnet. The developer needs records of the IP traffic to and from the instances' network interfaces, including rejected connections. Capturing the records must not add latency or reduce throughput on the application's network path. What should the developer turn on?
options: A packet capture agent on each instance that copies all IP traffic inline before forwarding it on.
VPC Flow Logs on the relevant network interfaces, published to CloudWatch Logs for analysis.
CloudTrail data events for the database so that each connection attempt is logged as an API call.
Database slow query logs that record the statements that took longest to finish on the instance.
questions.correct_rationale: Flow logs capture IP traffic information for network interfaces and are collected outside the traffic path, so they do not affect throughput or latency.
distractor_rationales: Inline capture records traffic, but copying packets on the path can add latency.
CloudTrail records API calls, not network connections to a database.
Slow query logs record statements, not rejected network connections.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options capture inline, log queries, or log API calls instead of traffic.

docLinks.title: Logging IP traffic using VPC Flow Logs

questions.subdomain: 4.1 Assist in a root cause analysis
questions.question: An API's error rate rose, and the access logs in CloudWatch Logs include the caller IP address on each request. The team must see which caller IPs produce the most error responses, ranked as a time series. They want a CloudWatch feature that evaluates the log data continuously, not a one-off query they rerun. What should the developer create?
options: A Logs Insights query that groups error lines by caller IP, saved and rerun by hand during incidents.
A Contributor Insights rule on the log group that uses the caller IP field as the contributor key.
A metric filter that counts error lines from all caller IPs together and graphs the total over time.
An X-Ray group that filters traces by HTTP status so that slow requests are shown on the service map.
questions.correct_rationale: Contributor Insights rules analyze log data to create time series of top-N contributors defined by log fields such as IP address.
distractor_rationales: A Logs Insights query can rank IPs, but it is a one-off query that must be rerun.
A metric filter is continuous, but it counts total errors and does not rank callers.
X-Ray groups filter traces and do not rank caller IPs from logs.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options rank once, count without ranking, or use traces instead of logs.

questions.subdomain: 4.2 Apply logging, monitoring, and observability best practices
questions.question: A team's Lambda concurrency use is growing, and they want warning before they reach the account quota so they can request an increase in time. What should they set up?
options: A reserved concurrency setting on every function equal to the account's whole concurrency quota.
A monthly calendar reminder to read the quota page and compare it with the team's current usage.
A support case opened every quarter that asks AWS to raise each quota whether or not it is needed.
A CloudWatch alarm from the Service Quotas console that alerts when usage nears the quota value.
questions.correct_rationale: Service Quotas lets you create CloudWatch alarms that notify you when you are close to a quota threshold.
distractor_rationales: Reserving the whole quota on each function is not possible and gives no warning.
A monthly manual check can miss growth between checks.
Routine increase requests do not warn about actual usage.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options rely on manual checks, misuse reserved concurrency, or skip monitoring.

questions.subdomain: 4.2 Apply logging, monitoring, and observability best practices
questions.question: A team uses CodeDeploy for its application deployments. Failure notifications must be driven by the deployment application's own events, not by someone watching the console, and must be set up once on the application rather than separately on each deployment group. The notifications must reach the team's email addresses subscribed to an SNS topic. What should the developer configure?
options: An EventBridge rule on the deployment state-change events that invokes a Lambda function to post to a chat channel.
An SNS topic with the team's emails, and a rota of developers who post to it after checking the console.
A notification rule in the Developer Tools console for the deployment application, targeting the SNS topic.
A CloudWatch dashboard that graphs deployment counts and is reviewed in the weekly team meeting.
questions.correct_rationale: Developer Tools notification rules watch resource events, such as deployment applications, and send to SNS topic targets.
distractor_rationales: The rule is event-driven, but it posts to a chat channel instead of the email addresses subscribed to the SNS topic.
The SNS topic reaches email, but people posting after console checks is not event-driven.
A weekly dashboard review is neither quick nor event-driven.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options miss the SNS email target, rely on people watching, or review weekly.

questions.subdomain: 4.2 Apply logging, monitoring, and observability best practices
questions.question: An ECS task runs an API container and a worker container, and the worker sometimes hangs while its process keeps running. ECS must mark the task unhealthy when the worker hangs, using a check that runs inside the worker container. The image's built-in Docker HEALTHCHECK is not being honored, and the fix must make ECS evaluate the check. What should the developer do?
options: Define a healthCheck command for the worker in the task definition and mark the worker as not essential.
Keep the HEALTHCHECK instruction in the image's Dockerfile and mark the worker container as essential.
Add an ALB target group health check on the API container's port to cover the worker container too.
Define a healthCheck command in the worker's container definition and keep the worker marked essential.
questions.correct_rationale: ECS monitors health checks specified in the container definition, and an unhealthy essential container makes the task unhealthy.
distractor_rationales: The check is evaluated, but only essential containers with health checks determine task health.
ECS does not monitor Docker health checks embedded in the image unless they are in the container definition.
An ALB check probes the API port and cannot see a hung worker process.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options rely on the image check, exclude the worker from task health, or probe the wrong container.

questions.subdomain: 4.3 Optimize applications by using AWS services and features
questions.question: A team runs hundreds of Lambda functions whose memory settings were picked by guesswork. They need memory recommendations based on each function's observed usage. They want an AWS service to produce these findings rather than load testing every function themselves. What should they use?
options: Amazon CloudWatch Lambda Insights, which collects each function's memory and CPU usage metrics for dashboards.
A custom harness that invokes each function at several memory sizes and records duration and cost.
AWS Compute Optimizer Lambda recommendations, which flag memory under- or over-provisioned functions.
Set every function to the maximum memory size so that no function is ever short of CPU or memory.
questions.correct_rationale: Compute Optimizer generates Lambda memory recommendations and flags functions as memory under-provisioned or over-provisioned.
distractor_rationales: Lambda Insights is an AWS feature that reports observed usage, but it gives metrics to interpret, not memory recommendations.
A harness measures usage, but it is the self-run testing the team wants to avoid.
Maximum memory wastes cost and is not a recommendation.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options test by hand, check the wrong resources, or overprovision everything.

questions.subdomain: 4.3 Optimize applications by using AWS services and features
questions.question: A web tier on EC2 behind an Application Load Balancer must scale with traffic. Scaling must keep the average request count per instance near a chosen value. The team does not want to create or tune the CloudWatch alarms that drive scaling. Which scaling policy fits?
options: A scheduled action that sets the group's desired capacity for business hours each weekday morning.
A target tracking policy on ALBRequestCountPerTarget with the chosen value as the target.
A target tracking policy on average CPU utilization of the group with the chosen value as the target.
A step scaling policy on ALBRequestCountPerTarget with alarms the team creates and tunes for each step.
questions.correct_rationale: Target tracking scales on a metric target value, Auto Scaling creates and manages the alarms, and ALBRequestCountPerTarget measures requests per instance.
distractor_rationales: Scheduled capacity does not track request count.
Target tracking manages alarms, but CPU does not hold request count per instance at the chosen value.
Step scaling can use the request metric, but the team must create and tune the alarms.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options use self-managed alarms, track the wrong metric, or follow a fixed schedule.

questions.subdomain: 4.3 Optimize applications by using AWS services and features
questions.question: A CloudFront distribution serves product images whose content does not depend on who is viewing, and its cache hit ratio is low. Viewers' session cookies, which are part of the cache key today, must stop splitting the cache. The image path must still identify each object in the cache so different images are never mixed up. What should the developer change?
options: Use a cache policy that removes cookies, headers, and the URL path, so all requests share one cache entry.
Lower the origin's response time so cache misses return faster even though the hit ratio stays the same.
Keep the URL path and the session cookie in the cache key, and raise the default TTL on the cache policy.
Use a cache policy that leaves the session cookie out of the cache key while keeping the URL path in it.
questions.correct_rationale: Including fewer values in the cache key raises the hit ratio, and the cache key is what identifies each cached object.
distractor_rationales: Removing the cookie helps hits, but dropping the path would let different images share one entry.
Faster misses do not raise the hit ratio.
The path still identifies each object, but the cookie keeps splitting the cache per viewer, so the hit ratio stays low.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options strip too much, add more key values, or tune the origin instead.

docLinks.title: Control the cache key with a policy

questions.subdomain: 4.3 Optimize applications by using AWS services and features
questions.question: An app must send each user a reminder exactly once at a user-chosen date and time in that user's time zone. Today a Lambda function runs every minute to scan a table for due reminders. Which change removes the polling?
options: Create an EventBridge Scheduler rate schedule per user that runs hourly and checks whether a reminder is due.
Create an EventBridge Scheduler one-time schedule per reminder with an at expression and user time zone.
Store reminders in an SQS queue with a delay set to the reminder time and process each message on arrival.
Keep the per-minute function but cache the reminders table in memory to make each scan faster.
questions.correct_rationale: EventBridge Scheduler one-time schedules invoke a target once at a specified date, time, and time zone.
distractor_rationales: An hourly rate schedule still polls and can be late.
SQS delays are far too short for user-chosen future dates.
Caching speeds the scan but keeps the polling.
questions.distractor_summary: The wrong options keep polling in some form or rely on a queue delay that cannot reach future dates.

lessons.title: Decoupling, Lambda configuration, and data stores
body: Synchronous integrations hold the caller's connection until the work finishes, so slow or fragile work belongs behind an asynchronous hand-off. Queues such as SQS buffer the work, retry failed deliveries, and park messages that keep failing in a dead-letter queue for inspection. Event-driven options — S3 event notifications, EventBridge rules, SNS fan-out — let consumers come and go without touching the producer.

Lambda functions are configured, not administered: memory, timeout, and concurrency shapes each function's behavior. Reserved concurrency caps (or reserves) how many instances may run at once, which protects downstream systems; provisioned concurrency pre-initializes instances so requests skip the cold-start wait. Functions in private subnets reach private resources directly and use VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB. Versions are immutable snapshots; aliases are movable pointers that pin environments.

Data stores follow access patterns. DynamoDB favors keyed access with a high-cardinality partition key; low-cardinality keys concentrate traffic on hot partitions. Reads are eventually consistent by default, with strongly consistent reads available per call. ElastiCache provides managed in-memory caching for microsecond-scale reads, and S3 lifecycle rules transition aging objects to cheaper storage and expire them on schedule.
decisions: Asynchronous hand-off through SQS, then return
Holding the connection until work finishes

lessons.title: Identity, encryption, secrets, and AI safety
body: Authentication for applications runs through Cognito user pools: they federate external identity providers such as SAML directories and issue short-lived tokens that your APIs accept. Identity pools are a different layer — they exchange tokens for temporary AWS service credentials. Workloads get their own temporary credentials from IAM roles: instance profiles on EC2, OIDC federation for CI systems, with trust policies scoping exactly who may assume them. Presigned URLs give out time-limited, per-object access instead of credentials.

Encryption at rest and in transit starts with KMS. For large payloads, envelope encryption is the pattern: KMS generates a data key, the application encrypts the data with it, and the wrapped data key travels with the object — decryption re-runs the IAM check. Secrets Manager rotates credentials on schedules and hands out the current value at runtime. CloudWatch Logs data protection policies detect and mask PII in log output while keeping records intact.

AI services add their own controls. Model access must be enabled per account and Region before a model can be invoked. Guardrails apply denied topics and PII redaction to prompts and responses. Interface VPC endpoints keep model traffic on private networking, and durable approval gates (a paused Step Functions task awaiting a callback) put a human between agents and destructive actions.

traps: User pools issue tokens for your APIs; identity pools issue AWS credentials — they are not interchangeable.
Encrypting a log group protects bytes at rest; it does not mask values from authorized readers.
IAM permissions alone do not authorize a Bedrock invocation — model access must be enabled first.
Guardrails filter content; they are not an authorization or human-approval mechanism.

lessons.title: Artifacts, configuration, testing, and CI/CD
body: Deployment artifacts come in shapes chosen for how they change. Lambda layers hold shared dependencies versioned separately from function code, so one build serves many functions. Container images fit teams whose Docker tooling and dependency sizes outgrow .zip packages, deployed through ECR. ECR lifecycle policies expire untagged and superseded images automatically while tag-based rules keep what production needs.

Configuration belongs outside the artifact. The same image promoted from development to production should read environment-specific settings from AWS AppConfig, which supports validation and gradual rollout strategies — a bad settings change rolls back through the rollout rather than flipping instantly. Lambda versions pin immutable snapshots and aliases repoint environments without redeploying.

Testing runs closest to the artifact locally: the SAM CLI invokes functions and serves APIs from the template before anything deploys. Mock integrations in API Gateway return agreed responses with no backend deployed. In the pipeline, CodePipeline promotes one artifact through stages, with manual approval actions recording sign-off before production. CodeDeploy's deployment configurations advance releases in batches and roll back automatically on CloudWatch alarms.

traps: $LATEST is a moving target — pin production to a version through an alias.

A schedule is not an approval — sign-off must be an audited gate in the pipeline.
Immutable tags prevent overwrites; they do not clean up superseded images.

lessons.title: Root cause, observability, and optimization
body: Root cause analysis starts with attribution. Metrics say that something is slow; traces say where. X-Ray records segments for each hop a request takes, so a latency spike in a path of API Gateway, functions, and queues is attributable per hop. When processing fails repeatedly, the dead-letter queue holds the evidence: its payloads show the defect, and after a fix the messages redrive back to the source queue instead of being replayed by hand. Build failures tell their cause in the build log — a version that resolves differently in CodeBuild than on a laptop points to un-pinned dependencies.

Observability practices make incidents searchable. Structured JSON logs with a correlation ID propagated from the API request let any tool filter one request's journey across hops. CloudWatch Logs Insights queries many log groups interactively and groups counts per service. Embedded metric format emits high-cardinality metrics — per tenant, per endpoint — asynchronously through log output, keeping the metrics API out of the hot path. Alarms on a dead-letter queue's message count page on-call engineers when processing fails.

Optimization respects constraints. Reserved concurrency caps concurrent executions to protect a downstream database. FIFO message groups give per-entity ordering while entities stay parallel. DAX serves DynamoDB reads from memory with minimal code change and passes strongly consistent reads through to the table.

traps: CloudTrail audits API calls; it does not trace request latency through your application.
An alarm on the source queue's age is not the same as paging when processing fails — watch the DLQ.
Debug logging everywhere adds volume without attributing latency to a hop.
ElastiCache requires application-managed cache logic; DAX serves DynamoDB reads with minimal changes.
